blocks.x: Vice Chair John Turcotte presided. Chair Larry McWilliams was absent (he'd flagged at the Oct. 6 meeting that this date falls on Election Day). Roll call: five of seven regular members — Turcotte, Kevin Price, Nancy Litrocapes, Jason Frazier, and Karen Axelson — answered present. Robin Tannenbaum was absent along with McWilliams. Both alternates, Oriana Farnham and Lucas Schrage, were also absent. They weren't needed for quorum (the minimum number of members needed to vote). The Oct. 6, 2026 minutes were adopted.
Quorum established; Oct. 6, 2026 minutes approved unanimously, 5–0. Mover and seconder not stated on the recording.
22-000604 — Site Plan Approval Extension — 860 Spring Street, Boulos Asset Management

The applicant is requesting a fourth extension of the approval granted on November 1, 2022, for a 15,240 sq. ft. building addition located at 860 Spring Street. The extension would move the approval date out by one year, through November 1, 2027. Tax Map 003, Lot 101A, Industrial Park District.

Jake of Sebago Technics, representing Boulos Asset Management, said the extension comes down to interest rates and the broader economy. No tenant has been found for the addition in three years. The applicant is hopeful construction can begin before the new deadline. Vice Chair Turcotte noted the board's informal practice (“you definitely get one, you probably get two… we're on the fourth”). He raised no objection given the financial constraints described. There was no public comment, on the floor or via Zoom. All findings, conclusions, and conditions from the 2022 approval remain in effect.
Approved unanimously, 5–0, by roll call. Mover and seconder not stated on the recording.
26-000847 — Land Use Ordinance Amendment, § 335-7.1 Village Review Overlay Zone (VROZ)

The proposed amendments include changes to the Village Review Overlay Zone review process. An overlay zone is a district with extra rules layered on top of the regular zoning. The changes are part of a city-wide initiative. The initiative reviews the structure and procedures of City boards, committees, and commissions for consistency with legal requirements and local practices.

Director Rebecca Spitella (Planning & Code Enforcement) explained that this continues a city-wide ordinance-modernization effort workshopped with the board last month. The standalone Village Review Overlay Zone (VROZ) advisory committee will be sunset (ended). Its design standards stay in the ordinance. But review of village-design applications moves into the Planning Board's own process, where it's recorded and more accessible to the public. Spitella said staff met with the VROZ committee. It recommended a broader, separate look at updating the VROZ standards themselves. Newer development often doesn't fit standards written for an earlier era. That update will return to the board in a future meeting. The amendment also narrows when a demolition inside the Village Review district needs Planning Board approval. It would apply only to structures listed in or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places. That way a deteriorating garage or shed isn't swept in alongside buildings of real historic significance. One board member asked whether giving the Chair a role in the demolition-approval recommendation process, as drafted, exists anywhere else in city ordinance. Spitella confirmed it does not. This would be a new role for the Chair.

“One of the things that I find valuable about [VROZ] is that they're just specifically focused on… that very specific set of ordinances. And when we bring this into the Planning Board, we're dealing with things that are all over the number of zones in the city… I don't know that we'd have the same luxury to focus in that deeply… I know that there's at least one architect and [a] historic preservationist [on VROZ] and they volunteer their time, right? Or they get a stipend or something. That's quite a gift to the community.”

Spitella responded that the shift reflects the board's own increased architectural focus over time. Spitella also said village-review items will still get a dedicated presentation and conversation at the Planning Board table, rather than being folded silently into a site plan review (the board's detailed review of a building project). Litrocapes acknowledged the explanation but maintained her view — “I still think that if there was an adjustment in those one or two meetings a year where [the] public could attend, I still find value in that committee” [12:44] — and no one else raised objections.
Recommended to City Council unanimously, 5–0, by roll call. Mover and seconder not stated on the recording.

Site Plan, Shoreland Zone (land near water, with extra rules): an 8-foot-wide multimodal (for more than one way of travel) riverwalk. It extends from the pedestrian bridge near Bridge Street to Garfield Street, along the Presumpscot River's north bank. Tax Map 032 and 039, Lots 223 and 031, City Center District and Residential Growth Area 1. Workshop only — no vote.

Craig Burgess (project consultant, on behalf of the City) said a conceptual plan for this stretch dates to 2015. He said the project in front of the board is “vastly different.” Environmental work began in 2018. Acorn Engineering was engaged in 2025. The team has held three public meetings. Two were neighborhood meetings in August and October 2025. One was in September 2026, tied to the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) review. The team also met with regulators including Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine DEP, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. A Maine DEP individual Natural Resources Protection Act permit application was submitted in October 2026. The major site plan application is expected back before the board for review in January 2027. Construction documents will be developed through 2027. Permit approvals are hoped for by March 2027. The brownfield-eligible first phase is to be complete by September 2028. The remainder of the project is to be finished by October 2029.

The City was awarded a $4 million U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Brownfields cleanup grant in 2025. Brownfields grants pay for cleaning up land with past contamination. The grant has a September 2028 sunset date (end date). Allie Druin (Credere Associates) said it is unlikely to be extended “given the current climate” at the federal EPA. The full $4 million is available for this project. A separate $300,000 in Westbrook Improvement Corporation seed funding covers costs that aren't Brownfields-eligible. Robyn Saunders (City Project Manager) put the likely full construction cost at roughly $8 million. That figure starts from the 2015 cost estimate (originally $5–7 million, for a different, unpermitted concept). It subtracts work no longer planned and applies a 5% annual escalator (a yearly cost increase). A firmer number is expected from a newly retained cost estimator by the end of 2026.

Allie Druin (Credere Associates) said 2023 soil sampling found sporadic, marginal exceedances of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and some metals above Maine DEP remedial action guidelines (cleanup limits) along the corridor. It was not a single hot spot, so the whole stretch is treated as similarly affected. Rather than excavating soil along the riverbank, the remedial approach is to prevent exposure through engineering controls. These include keeping people on the boardwalk above the soil, maintaining vegetation to limit erosion and disturbance, and an operation-and-maintenance plan requiring ongoing inspection. For the long term, an environmental covenant will run with the property. That covenant satisfies a Maine DEP “no action assurance” letter that protects the City from future liability for the existing contamination.

The trail links Cornelia Warren Fields, Riverbank Park, and the forthcoming Saccarappa Park. It combines an on-grade (ground-level) asphalt path with elevated boardwalk sections. The boardwalk sections span steep slopes and wetlands with minimal disturbance. A “parklet” is planned at a wider section of the site. It is outside both the river's 25-foot setback (the required distance from the river) and delineated wetlands. It is meant to let people step off the boardwalk and experience the river directly. Three site areas will test invasive-species control methods (Japanese knotweed, multiflora rose, Norway maple) before the rest of the corridor is treated. Lighting, security/emergency call boxes, seating, guardrail height, screening from abutting yards, and trash management are all still being studied. The boardwalk's decking material hasn't been chosen yet. The choice balances durability against cost, and the existing South Riverwalk's wood is in poor shape.

Vice Chair Turcotte said he had thought the trail would go to the bridge. He asked whether it turns up Garfield Street because Water Street is too close to the water. He said he saw the team nodding. In answer to questions from Jason Frazier, the team said the elevated boardwalk sits entirely above the 100-year floodplain (only the helical pier foundations extend below it). Staff (Rebecca Spitella) said the parcel is public land rather than a right-of-way (public land along a road). Staff said it would presumably follow park rules with dawn-to-dusk hours. Those hours don't necessarily apply to every part of the existing Riverwalk, such as the stretch behind the restaurants. Turcotte also suggested matching the lighting design to the South Riverwalk “since we'll be looking across at each other.”

“I live in an area where… the belief [is] that if you don't put a trash bin there, people will carry out their trash. I can tell you it's not true. There's trash constantly around the bus stop and there's no trash bin.”

(Litrocapes was referring to a Metro bus stop on Mechanic Street that has had no trash bin for 16 years.) Karen Axelson asked how much of the $4 million EPA grant is available for this project (see Funding above). Litrocapes also raised design continuity between the new North Riverwalk and the existing South Riverwalk, since the rendering shown didn't match. The team explained the two banks have genuinely different site conditions (the river's “cut bank” geometry differs on the south side). The team said it is already discussing shared wayfinding (signs that help people find their way) and interpretive signage, and possibly art installations, to tie the two halves together. Litrocapes also asked how much of the existing tree canopy and river view would be preserved. The team said its intent is to keep the boardwalk pushed back from the river's high-water line, preserve the shoreline's existing silver maples, and revegetate any disturbed area. On trash/amenities, the team said benches and receptacles, if added, would most likely be concentrated at the parklet and the trail's end points. They would not be along the narrow 8-foot boardwalk itself, which needs to stay clear for emergency/utility vehicle access. The team noted that bus-stop bins are Metro's responsibility and a different situation from the Riverwalk. The team said they weren't dismissing Litrocapes's point: “Let's have a community conversation about it. Thank you.”
No vote — workshop item. The major site plan application is expected to return to the board for formal review in January 2027.
